header:
Date/Time: 2026-07-09 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Marcus Vega (Redwood AE), Anika Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Head of ML, DataLoom), Tom Rivera (Platform Eng), Evelyn Morris (SRE)
summary: POC scoping focused on integrating DataLoom's benchmark harness with Redwood's load testing. Discussed success criteria (latency P95/P99, cost per 1M tokens, quality/regression thresholds), workload sizing (token length distributions, concurrency), streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs, and timeline for a 1-week load test on dedicated capacity. Agreed next steps: share harness repo, customer to provide traces and scripts, SE to produce test matrix.
topics: Load testing approach - streaming vs non-streaming
Dedicated capacity vs hosted - config and cost implications
transcript:
[00:00] Marcus Vega: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Marcus from Redwood, I'm AE on the account. We got Anika from SE here. Quick intros?
[00:18] Priya Shah: Hi, Priya here, Head of ML at DataLoom. We'll drive the POC.
[00:28] Tom Rivera: Tom, platform engineer, I'll own the integration bits.
[00:34] Anika Patel: Hi all, Anika, technical lead for inference at Redwood. I'll help with the harness and tests.
[00:42] Evelyn Morris: Evelyn, SRE, mostly here for the load and reliability side.
[00:50] Marcus Vega: Great. Goal for today: align on benchmark planning, what scripts you have, and streaming vs non-streaming differences, plus timeline.
[01:05] Priya Shah: Yeah, we want to validate latency SLOs and cost at scale. Our internal success criteria are P95 < 300ms for single-turn summaries and P99 < 700ms for longer conversations, and keep cost under X per million tokens — we'll share the exact number.
[01:23] Anika Patel: Helpful — when you say summaries: average input token length and output token length?
[01:30] Priya Shah: Typical input is 120 tokens, average output 80 tokens for summary tasks. For chat flow, sequences can be 2k to 6k tokens occasionally — largely due to context.
[01:42] Tom Rivera: We have traces from last quarter showing median ctx length 600 tokens but tail to 6k. I'll upload histograms.
[01:50] Marcus Vega: Perfect. That informs batching and KV cache sizing. A couple of clarifications up front: are you planning to run streaming responses in prod, or buffered (non-streaming)?
[02:06] Priya Shah: Prefer streaming for UX, but if latency costs blow up we might consider buffered. Part of the POC is to show tradeoffs.
[02:15] Anika Patel: Ok noted. For the harness: do you already have scripts that hit your prompt templates, or do you want us to stand up the harness and run against synthetic traffic?
[02:25] Tom Rivera: We have a set of JMeter-like scripts and a small harness in Python. It's not Redwood-specific. Ideally we can plug those in, but we can also adapt.
[02:35] Marcus Vega: Good. Our benchmark harness repo has a runner that can accept a JSONL of requests, concurrency config, and a streaming toggle. We'll share the repo link and an example script.
[02:46] Priya Shah: Will those scripts preserve session state for multi-turn tests?
[02:52] Anika Patel: Yes — the harness has session support. It will re-send previous turns as context, or you can supply KV-cache warmup traces to simulate cache hits. We often run two phases: cold-start (no cache) and warmed (simulate prior KV cache).
[03:07] Evelyn Morris: How do you simulate KV cache hits?
[03:11] Anika Patel: You can provide a sequence of requests for each session; the harness keeps the session key and replays the prompt history. There's also a fast path where we preload the model's KV cache for certain sessions to measure steady-state throughput.
[03:25] Tom Rivera: That preloading is important; our users expect low latency during active sessions. Can you reproduce the same warm cache conditions as our prod traffic?
[03:34] Anika Patel: We'll need representative traces from you — token boundaries, role markers, timestamps help. If you can't provide exact traces, a synthetic warmup that mimics token lengths and distribution works.
[03:47] Marcus Vega: From a timeline standpoint, we'd like to do a dry run the week of July 20th and a focused 1-week load test after prep. Does that align?
[03:57] Priya Shah: Sounds good. We might need a little time to sanitize traces for PII.
[04:02] Evelyn Morris: We'll scrub PII and replace with placeholders.
[04:06] Anika Patel: Great — regarding streaming vs non-streaming, tradeoffs: streaming reduces perceived latency for the user but can slightly increase resource usage and complicate batching. Non-streaming (buffered) lets the runtime batch better and sometimes reduces cost per token. We'll prepare benchmarks showing both.
[04:22] Priya Shah: We care about both perceived latency and cost. Can you show P50/P95/P99 for both modes and also token throughput?
[04:31] Anika Patel: Yes. We'll report latency distributions, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and cost estimates for Dedicated vs Hosted. Also we'll include quality checks (sampled outputs compared to a baseline and Rouge/BLEU-like metrics).
[04:44] Tom Rivera: For quality regression checks, do you support automated evals in the harness?
[04:50] Anika Patel: The harness can run eval scripts you provide; we can compute exact-match, BLEU, Rouge, or embed-based similarity. We also support human-in-the-loop flags to mark suspicious regressions.
[04:58] Marcus Vega: On capacity: do you want to run this on Dedicated reserved nodes or on hosted? Dedicated gives predictable throughput, which is useful for stress tests.
[05:08] Priya Shah: For the 1-week full-scale run, Dedicated sounds preferable. How much reserved capacity should we request for a realistic test?
[05:16] Anika Patel: Based on your traces — median ctx 600, tail to 6k, concurrency target?
[05:23] Tom Rivera: We aim for 120 concurrent active sessions at peak, with average 2 requests/min per session, but spikes to 500 concurrent in flash sale scenarios.
[05:33] Anika Patel: We'll propose a config: start with 4 GPUs with autoscale bump to 8 for spikes for the test window. We'll also run a microbenchmark to map tokens/sec per GPU for your model/quantization profile.
[05:45] Priya Shah: Speaking of models, we're evaluating both open models and some hosted off-the-shelf. We'll give you model names, but expect quantized variants. Does Redwood support 4-bit/8-bit quantized runs in the harness?
[05:58] Anika Patel: Yes, the runtime supports int8 and custom 4-bit paths; we'll supply kernels chosen per model. For benchmarks, we'll compare full-fp16 vs quantized profiles so you can see cost/latency tradeoffs.
[06:10] Marcus Vega: On observability: we'll provide logs and traces; what kind of metrics should you ingest from our side to correlate?
[06:18] Evelyn Morris: We can ship AI request traces, Prometheus metrics, and GPU-level metrics.
[06:23] Anika Patel: GPU metrics, request ids, and timestamps are sufficient. Include role tags and session ids so we can measure per-session P95. We'll also need a mapping of prompt templates to test cases.
[06:36] Tom Rivera: We'll add template ids and map them to the JSONL requests.
[06:41] Priya Shah: One concern: network egress and data residency. We'll likely run POC in our AWS region in us-east-1 but need encryption and KMS controls.
[06:51] Marcus Vega: For Dedicated, we can deploy in your VPC and integrate with your KMS. We'll share the Private deployment checklist. For hosted runs we can enable encryption at rest and TLS in transit, but VPC is the way to go for full control.
[07:06] Priya Shah: Good. For pass/fail criteria: besides latency and cost, we want no functional regressions vs our baseline on a 200-sample eval set, and error rate under 0.2% (errors like timeouts or 5xx).
[07:18] Anika Patel: We'll include those checks and will set automatic abort thresholds for the test if errors exceed configured limits.
[07:26] Tom Rivera: How will you measure streaming perceived latency vs buffered?
[07:30] Anika Patel: Two metrics: time-to-first-byte (TTFB) and time-to-final-token. Streaming will show lower TTFB typically. We'll surface both, and also compute user-perceived latency using a heuristic where we consider the time until the first meaningful token.
[07:46] Priya Shah: Nice. Another implementation question: can your harness simulate backpressure and client disconnects to test graceful degradation?
[07:54] Anika Patel: Yes, we have a mode to randomly abort sessions, throttle connections, and test fallback to smaller models. We'll show fallback scenarios and automated routing by policy.
[08:06] Marcus Vega: Let's cover deliverables: Marcus will send the harness link and a short README with example scripts; Anika will send the test matrix showing streaming vs non-streaming configs and the proposed Dedicated sizing; DataLoom uploads traces and sample prompts. Then we schedule the dry run week of July 20th.
[08:26] Priya Shah: Agreed. Can you also provide an estimate of cost for the 1-week test so we can budget?
[08:31] Marcus Vega: We'll include a ballpark in the follow-up, plus exact breakdown by GPU-hour and estimated token consumption.
[08:38] Evelyn Morris: On security docs: send SOC2 and network diagrams — we'll need to review for the VPC setup.
[08:44] Marcus Vega: We'll attach SOC2, ISO binder, and our private deployment checklist.
[08:49] Tom Rivera: One more nit: our platform has per-route throttles and we need to validate that Redwood can honor header-based routing for rate limits.
[08:58] Anika Patel: Yes we can configure route-level policies; please include example headers in the test traces.
[09:05] Priya Shah: Anything else?
[09:08] Marcus Vega: Quick note on reporting: we'll deliver a benchmark report with metrics, sample outputs, cost estimates, and recommended model/quantization profile.
[09:17] Priya Shah: That's perfect. Thanks everyone.
[09:21] Marcus Vega: Thanks — we'll follow up with links and schedule.
[09:25] (end)
